from: The direct proof constructs two distributions on the whole sign cube. The first is uniform. The second is obtained by rounding a chain of correlated Gaussian vectors to signs. Their Forrelation means differ, but a shallow decision tree has nearly the same expectation under both distributions. To prove this indistinguishability, scale only the first block of Gaussian biases. Differentiation starts in that block; Gaussian integration by parts then moves the derivative through one coordinate of each successive block. Every attempted return to a coordinate already differentiated vanishes by multilinearity. The resulting order-$k$ derivative sum is controlled by a martingale along the decision tree.
to: Two moment estimates turn this expectation comparison into a promise lower bound. Because neither distribution is entirely supported on the promise, the algorithm is first amplified, and its behavior on unpromised inputs is bounded only by the interval $[0,1]$. The same estimates give a uniform numerical lower bound. Comparing that bound with $L_{k,m}$ proves (F3).

from: Adaptivity does not change the conditional distribution of a fresh coordinate. A reachable root-to-node path specifies exactly the values of its distinct queried coordinates. Conversely, every input with those values follows that path, by induction through the tree. The path event is therefore a cylinder under the original product measure. All unqueried coordinates retain their independent laws on that event. In particular, (F27) is a centered increment conditional on the query history.
to: Equivalently, the right side is the sum over reachable leaves of their cylinder probabilities times their output and terminal chaos. Each leaf probability is the product of the answer probabilities at its distinct queried coordinates; a repeated query contributes no additional factor. A zero-probability leaf contributes zero, so this finite-sum proof does not condition on a null event.
